description:
## Question

What do Nx (defn, Nx.Defn.Evaluator, EXLA, Torchx) and other existing Elixir libraries already do well for loop-heavy and numeric work, and where they don't fit (scalar loops with early exit, small inputs, data dependencies between iterations, byte processing, startup cost, scheduler behaviour)? Output: the boundary between Nx's niche and the jobs left for something like defk, with sources.

comments.text:
Research findings: branch research/nx-boundary, docs/research/nx-boundary.md. Summary: Nx (1.0) owns whole-tensor, fixed-shape, batched numerics (reductions, windows, scans, linalg, conv, grads, GPU); defk should not compete there.
Gaps Nx leaves: (1) sequential scalar loops with data dependencies or early exit. defn has only while (no recursion, no break), its docs say to avoid hand loops, XLA while is sequential (nx#122), and on the default Evaluator it is interpreted op by op.
(2) Variable-length or small inputs at high call rates. defn compiles once per shape, the jit cache lookup 'may take milliseconds', every EXLA call takes a per-device GenServer lock (one host device by default), and empty tensors are not allowed.
(3) Bytes and integer-exact work. There are no dynamic shapes (no masking or filtering), ints wrap silently, and integer div by zero is UB.
(4) Scheduling. EXLA and Torchx run as dirty NIFs and EMLX on worker threads. None of them yields, and per ERTS a dirty NIF keeps running after its process is killed. Only the pure-Elixir Evaluator is preemptible.
defk's yielding on normal schedulers is the property no Nx backend offers.

title: Where does Nx already cover native-speed numerics for Elixir?
